predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper calls R a "data rate" and states R = log2(1+SNR). This is only the capacity normalized by complex-channel use (or by Hz under specified normalization), not a physical data rate. For bandwidth B, the AWGN capacity is C = B log2(1 + P/(N0 B)) bits/s under the usual conventions. It is also an upper bound achieved only with appropriate coding, not a fundamental equality for the proposed modulation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraphs beginning "Transmit beamforming is a spatial repetition code" and "Let all data be repeated T times"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript labels transmit beamforming a repetition code of rate 1/N and says it gives an SNR gain of N. A single-stream beamformer transmits one stream per channel use; it is not a rate-1/N code in the normal coding-rate sense. Its array gain depends critically on the power normalization: with fixed total transmit power, coherent MISO beamforming has an N-fold received-power gain relative to one antenna; with fixed power per antenna, total power rises by N and the coherent received power can scale as N^2. The text gives neither normalization, yet compares this directly with temporal repetition.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph beginning "Information theory does not care, if we exchange space and time"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed space--time interchange is not generally information-theoretically or operationally equivalent. Spatial beamforming uses antennas simultaneously, while repetition consumes T channel uses, reduces throughput at fixed bandwidth, adds latency, and requires the fading channel to remain coherent over the repetitions. A multi-antenna channel also has a channel vector and potentially spatial degrees of freedom, unlike a scalar AWGN channel. Equivalence would require explicitly matched total-energy, bandwidth, latency, channel-coherence, and CSI assumptions; none are supplied. Therefore the claim cannot justify making transmit beamforming "dispensable."

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, statement "In time domain, data symbols are conveniently separated by orthogonality via pulse shaping"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Ordinary pulse shaping does not by itself make adjacent transmitted symbols orthogonal. Raised-cosine/Nyquist pulse shaping provides zero ISI only at prescribed sampling instants under synchronization; the continuous-time shifted pulses are generally not orthogonal. This is especially not a valid generic contrast to frequency multiplexing.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section II, paragraph beginning "In that regime, you can hardly do anything better than concatenating... repetition coding"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Low-SNR AWGN capacity being approximately linear in SNR does not imply that repetition coding is nearly optimal or necessary. Repetition increases post-combining SNR only by spending additional channel uses/energy and correspondingly lowers spectral efficiency. Capacity-approaching low-rate codes need not be constructed by appending repetition codes. The asserted near-optimality is unsupported and is false without a narrowly specified complexity, latency, and code-family constraint.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section II, paragraph beginning "For low-rate repetition coding... restricting to phase modulation has a very similar effect as a repetition code of rate one half"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The statement is presented as a general AWGN result but lacks a power constraint, definition of phase modulation, and a capacity or error-exponent calculation. Constant-envelope phase-only signaling has a different constrained input alphabet from temporal repetition. Although both can have a one-real-dimension high-SNR prelog under particular normalizations, their finite-SNR capacities and energy efficiencies are not generally equivalent; the claimed low-SNR disappearance is not established.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section III, paragraph beginning "GSM is standardized with minimum shift keying as modulation format"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: GSM specifies Gaussian minimum-shift keying (GMSK), conventionally with BT = 0.3 and differential encoding, not bare MSK as its modulation format. GMSK is deliberately a filtered CPM variant and is not interchangeable with unfiltered MSK. The wording is materially misleading because the subsequent argument relies on the Gaussian filtering and differential precoding that distinguish GSM GMSK from MSK.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section III, paragraph beginning "Consider a quaternary minimum shift keying... Both quadrature components can be demodulated independently"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Replacing binary CPM phase increments by the four increments {±pi/4, ±3pi/4} does not yield two independently demodulable QPSK quadrature components. CPM forms exp(j phi(t)) from the accumulated, pulse-shaped phase; the in-phase and quadrature observations are consequently coupled through the nonlinear phase state and CPM memory. Independent I/Q demodulation would require a demonstrated special decomposition and receiver model, neither of which is given. A Gray label on the four increments does not establish such separability.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section III, paragraph claiming an "at most 37% wider" spectrum and "at least 46%" spectral-efficiency boost
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The numerical spectral-efficiency conclusion is not well-defined or demonstrated. Gaussian-filtered CPM has nonzero spectral tails and therefore no unique finite bandwidth. The manuscript does not specify an occupied-bandwidth criterion, PSD integration threshold, symbol rate, detection penalty, or carrier-spacing constraint. The asserted 46% is merely 2/1.37 - 1 and is valid only if the unsubstantiated 37% bandwidth ratio is measured under a common explicit criterion; it cannot be inferred from a qualitative reference to a sidelobe shoulder.
